Goshintou Ceremony (also: Goshintou, Goushintou): The Goshintou Ceremony is a solemn Inazuman rite honouring the arrival of the Shogun, who according to tradition brought the knowledge of sword-making to the land. Master swordsmiths present their finest blades, called Goshintou, which are offered to the Grand Narukami Shrine. The swords stand for the union of human craft and the Shogun's divine favour.

Canon says very little about it directly: the best source is a passage in the Inazuman novel Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi, and no quest shows the ceremony being held.

Practice: Per the book, the ceremony began after thousands of years and many harvests, when mortal smiths could at last forge swords pleasing even to Narukami. The Grand Narukami Shrine and the Shogunate then gathered the greatest swords in the world and offered them to the shrine, and the blades so offered were named Goshintou. The book calls the occasion lively and says the custom continues in the present.

The book adds a hidden side to the tradition. A famous craftsman never makes a single blade in one sitting. The very best work is a Shinuchi, given a fine name and presented to the craftsman's lord or deity; it is not made for taking lives and stays pure. Other blades from the same smith are Kageuchi, given to retainers as working weapons that will shed blood and be stained. The author says few people know these behind-the-scenes matters. The book does not say outright that Goshintou are always Shinuchi, though that is the natural reading of the passage.

Regional variation: No regional variation is described. The offering goes to the Grand Narukami Shrine on Narukami Island, the seat of the Electro Archon's worship, so the rite belongs to the Shogunate's heartland rather than to Watatsumi, Tsurumi or other islands with their own faiths.

Scene use: Use it as background colour for Inazuman sword culture: a smith talking about preparing a piece worthy of the shrine, a collector explaining the difference between Shinuchi and Kageuchi, or a priest of the shrine receiving a blade. Keep dates, rankings and rules vague unless the scene invents them clearly as local detail, since canon gives none.

Characters who know the book can repeat its version of the origin story, but should treat it as popular legend: it is a novel that was once restricted, and Ei herself calls its later parts idealised. A character close to the Shrine or Shogunate would present the ceremony simply as a respectful custom, with no claim about what the Shogun thinks of it.

1.content:
In the account given by Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi, a master smith's best sword is a Shinuchi, named and offered to a lord or deity and kept free of bloodshed, while the other swords from the same forging are Kageuchi, issued to retainers and used in battle. Goshintou are the swords offered to the Grand Narukami Shrine; the book frames the offering as the origin of the name.

The same passage ties the terms to the first Shogun and her younger twin, Shin and Kage, light and dark; this is spoiler-adjacent context for the novel's title. See the book's own entry for that story.

Great Meeting of a Hundred Tales
2.content:
Hyakkiyakou (also: Night Parade of a Hundred Demons, Hyakumonogatari Daikai, Great Meeting of a Hundred Tales): The Hyakkiyakou (the "night parade of a hundred demons") was a gathering of Inazuma's youkai in an age when the land was thick with them. It grew out of parties organised by the Kitsune Saiguu, where guests drank and told stories into the small hours. It has not been held for centuries. In Version 2.5 Yae Miko staged one last, ritual version as a farewell for youkai memories.

The name works on two levels: hyakumonogatari daikai ("great meeting of a hundred tales") for the storytelling party, hyakkiyakou for what it turned into once the guests were drunk. The tradition is bound up with Yae Miko's own youth and her old friends among the kitsune.

Practice: Yae Miko explains that the Kitsune Saiguu would host gatherings where everyone drank and told stories late into the night, and that this became known as the hyakumonogatari daikai. Once the guests were properly drunk, they competed to cover the night sky with their powers, and the event came to be called the hyakkiyakou. Youkai were so numerous then that their silhouettes could block out the moon.

Miko describes it simply as a gathering of youkai, not something sinister, though she admits the name sounds ominous. Youkai normally rose into the sky under their own power; the guests were competing, so spectacle and drink were the point.

History: The Hyakkiyakou belongs to the era when Inazuma was full of youkai and the Kitsune Saiguu presided over its gatherings. Many youkai died in the Cataclysm and their bloodlines thinned, so the gathering lapsed and had not been held for centuries by the present day.

The old festival culture is shared with others of the period, such as the Mikawa Flower Festival, which youkai also held in those days.

Farewell 2 5: In Yae Miko's Story Quest (The Great Narukami Offering, Divina Vulpes Chapter Act I), a novel with a real summoning incantation circulates in Inazuma City. It was written by Urakusai, a kitsune and old friend of Miko, who had died and whose memories, along with those of other youkai, had leaked from the Ley Lines after rifthounds damaged the Sacred Sakura's roots in Transient Dreams. Urakusai possessed a struggling novelist to write it so that lingering youkai spirits could enjoy a last taste of life and leave without regret. When Miko meets him through the Traveler he asks for one more Hyakkiyakou for himself and the others, and she promises it.

Because the youkai memories are weak and can no longer fly, Miko performs a convocation ritual at the Grand Narukami Shrine, with the shrine maidens evacuated to avoid anyone being possessed and the Traveler clearing monsters stirred up on the way to Mt. Yougou. Miko, the Traveler and Paimon recite the incantation together as the youkai ascend, and readers of the novel across Inazuma City join in. The sky above the shrine fills with youkai memories, blocking the moon as in the old days, and they depart peacefully. No wishes are granted by the incantation, and the craze for novels containing incantations fades afterwards.

Scene use: Use it as nostalgic background for Yae Miko, kitsune or old youkai: a rowdy, affectionate night of sake, stories and showing off. For a modern scene it can only be a memory or a ritual remembrance, since living youkai in numbers are gone.

Keep the tone bittersweet. Do not invent rules, dates or a formal programme for the original event, and do not claim that wishes can be granted by it.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Hyakkiyakou is not held as a regular festival. The one revival in canon is the 2.5 farewell ritual; Miko and Urakusai treated it as a final one.

3.content: Urakusai was a cultured kitsune known for his literary works, once an associate of the Kitsune Saiguu and a grandfather figure to the young Yae Miko. His memories lingered in the Ley Lines after his death. He wrote the summoning novel in 2.5 so spirits could leave with a farewell, and asked Miko for a last Hyakkiyakou.

4.content:
Inazuman Arts (also: Arts of Inazuma, Inazuma arts and crafts, Inazuman culture of the arts): Inazuman arts mix refined pastimes and working crafts. Flower arrangement (ikebana) is a polished accomplishment of the noble Kamisato house. Poetry is honoured through the legend of the Five Kasen, the ancient poets remembered at the Irodori Festival. Printing and popular fiction are a major trade, led by Yae Publishing House. Bladesmithing is the most famous craft, descended from five forging schools called the Raiden Gokaden, of which only the Amenoma Art still thrives.

Two of these traditions are tied to the nation's wounds. The Gokaden collapsed through a conspiracy generations ago, and the nation's reopening after the Sakoku Decree revived its public arts, including the festival and the publishing contests. Martial arts have their own entry.

Practice: Ikebana is the art of arranging flowers into a composed display. The wiki's culture page lists Kamisato Ayaka and Fushizome as practitioners; Ayaka's profile counts flower arrangement among the disciplines she has mastered alongside tea ceremony, Go, music, poetry and dance, and she was preparing ikebana lessons during the 2.6 event.

Poetry and song hold a legendary place. The Five Kasen were gifted poets of ancient Inazuma who, in turns, presented a yearly collection to the Shogun, and their works are said to have helped Inazuman culture blossom. Stage plays once retold their story with each figure dressed in one colour, so audiences named them by colour.

Printing is described as one of Inazuma's main trades. Yae Publishing House, founded by Yae Miko, is known across Teyvat as a giant of the industry and periodically holds the "This Novel Is Amazing!" competition.

Bladesmithing is the nation's signature craft. Inazuman swords were famed enough to bring steady trade from Fontaine, and the best-known material is jade steel from Tatarasuna, though production halted after the peace between Watatsumi and the Shogunate.

The Raiden Gokaden ("Five Traditions of Raiden") were five smithing schools, each with its own forging art and closely guarded techniques; variation is said to come from astrology, materials, furnace conditions, the smith's character and elemental changes. The five were the Amenoma, Isshin, Futsu, Hyakume and Senju Arts. Their families became important within the Yashiro Commission because swordsmithing mattered so much to Inazuma's culture.

The Goshintou Ceremony honours the Shogun's arrival and the sword-making she brought: master smiths present their finest swords, goshintou, to the Grand Narukami Shrine as an offering. This detail comes from an in-game book cited on the wiki.

Yae Publishing House's catalogue appears across Teyvat. It publishes "A Legend of Sword" (written by Xingqiu under the pen name Zhenyu and illustrated by Albedo as Calx), "Legend of the Shattered Halberd" by Mr. Nine, and a long-running serial, "The Soulblazer Saga", with spin-offs and merchandise. Its columnists include "Ms. Hina". Chang the Ninth, a Liyue author, wrote an entry for the competition, mixing Liyue and Inazuman storytelling.

Regional variation: Within the Inazuma archipelago the crafts vary by place. Narukami Island and Inazuma City hold the publishing house, noble households and the Amenoma Smithy. Tatarasuna was the centre of jade-steel forging, with the Mikage Furnace; both are now closed or halted. Watatsumi Island's shrine maidens wear blue where those of Narukami wear red, and the island has its own army and clan crest.

Outside Inazuma the arts are carried by export and by foreign admirers: Fontaine buys Inazuman blades, Liyue and Natlan readers follow Yae Publishing House serials, and visiting writers and artists take part in its events.

History: The Five Kasen belong to the distant past, and much about them was lost in the cataclysm five hundred years ago. During the Sakoku Decree, trade and exports dropped sharply; after it was repealed the economy and public arts began to recover, and the Irodori Festival was revived in the limited-time Hues of the Violet Garden event (2.6).

The Raiden Gokaden were broken apart in the Case of the Eccentric: three schools vanished through "mishaps", the Isshin Art's smiths fled after failing to forge a sacred blade, and a man calling himself Kunikuzushi beat Kaedehara Yoshinori and the Kamisato head who pursued them. Only the Amenoma Art continues, led by Amenoma Tougo with Hajime as his pupil.

The Isshin Art had been ordered to recreate a sacred blade from a diagram sent by the Shogun; its smiths could not forge a working sword and fled to Snezhnaya for fear of punishment. The diagram had been tampered with by Kunikuzushi. Yoshinori and the Kamisato head kept the truth secret; the Kamisato head died soon after, the Yashiro Commission and the Kamisato Clan lost standing, and Yoshinori ended the Isshin Art.

The attacker's own origin is tied to Tatarasuna. Years earlier a kabukimono befriended the smith Niwa Hisahide, who ran the Mikage Furnace. Il Dottore, disguised as the Fontaine mechanic Escher, manipulated the furnace crisis; Niwa died, and a false tale blamed Niwa's flight on cowardice. The kabukimono later, as a Fatui agent, planned the fall of the Gokaden in revenge on an unspecified bladesmith. This is the original history; the Wanderer's own story and the Irminsul revision are covered elsewhere.

Yoshinori recorded the truth in ink that appeared only on contact with water. Kamisato Ayato found it while investigating a Fatui spy, then staged a fabricated Five Kasen legend during the festival to lead Kazuha to it. This is a limited-time event (2.6).

Scene use: Use Inazuman arts for quiet, cultured scenes: a flower-arranging lesson in a noble estate, a bookstall at Yae Publishing House, a poetry contest, or a smith's workshop at the Amenoma Smithy. Smiths and the Kamisato household treat the Gokaden's fall as a sensitive subject; the full story is known only to those who read Yoshinori's letter or lived the events. Writers and editors are enthusiastic and commercial rather than solemn.

Do not give the Five Kasen real names or fixed works; present them as legend. Keep Ayato's fabricated poems separate from any ancient text. Do not make the Gokaden a single unified guild that still exists.

Examples: Examples include Kamisato Ayaka's flower arrangement, the poems and plays of the Five Kasen, "A Legend of Sword" and "The Soulblazer Saga" from Yae Publishing House, jade-steel blades from Tatarasuna, and the sacred swords offered at the Goshintou Ceremony.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Amenoma Art survives under Amenoma Tougo, while the other four Gokaden schools are lost or nearly lost. Yae Publishing House remains a leading publisher. The Irodori Festival is shown once in canon (2.6) and its later schedule is unstated.

5.content:
The Raiden Gokaden were five Inazuman forging schools: Amenoma, Isshin, Futsu, Hyakume and Senju. Only the Amenoma Art, led by Amenoma Tougo, still trains new smiths; the Isshin Art barely survives; the rest are lost. The fall followed the Case of the Eccentric, in which a man calling himself Kunikuzushi defeated Kaedehara Yoshinori and the Kamisato head after tampering with a sacred-blade diagram.

The Isshin Art was held by the Kaedehara, Niwa and Akame families, and its three masters were known as the Isshin Sansaku. The origin of the schools is disputed between a ronin teaching five disciples and the Shogun's teaching.

6.content: Yae Publishing House is Inazuma's giant of the printing trade, founded and led by Yae Miko, who also serves as editor-in-chief. It runs the "This Novel Is Amazing!" contest and publishes serials such as "A Legend of Sword" and "The Soulblazer Saga". Its authors include Xingqiu (as Zhenyu) and Mr. Nine; Albedo has illustrated under the name Calx.

7.content: Ancient Inazuman poets whose names are colour-based stage names: Suikou (green), Aoi no Okina (blue), Akahito (red), Sumizome (white) and Kuronushi (black). Their true lives are lost. The poem series told in the 2.6 event, The Five Kasen's Splendor, was written by Kamisato Ayato to guide Kazuha to a hidden family secret.

8.content: A solemn Inazuman ceremony recalling the Shogun's arrival and the sword-making she brought. Master swordsmiths present their finest blades, goshintou, as offerings to the Grand Narukami Shrine. Known from an in-game book, not from a shown event.

9.content:
Inazuma Cuisine (also: Inazuman food, Inazuman cuisine, Inazuma dishes): Inazuman food is light and built on fresh ingredients. Rice is the staple grain, eaten steamed or pounded into rice cakes that can be sweet or savoury. As on any island nation, fish, shrimp, crab, eel and seaweed fill many traditional dishes. Noodles (udon, soba, ramen) are loved, and sakura, a flavour tied to Inazuma, appears in both sweets and savouries. The best-known eating place is Kiminami Restaurant in Inazuma City.

Red meat and poultry mostly appear in imported dishes rather than traditional ones. Food is also a lively part of street and festival life: stalls sell snacks such as dango, and the Kamisato Clan has long ordered meals from the same city restaurant. Poor soil on some islands limits what can be grown locally.

The Vision Hunt and Sakoku decrees strained supplies and trade for everyone in Inazuma, and the end of the sakoku policy reopened contact with foreign ingredients and dishes. Since then foreign dishes such as pizza have been adapted by local cooks.

Practice: Rice is central. Tricolor Dango is a soft steamed rice-flour sweet; Rice Cake Soup is a savoury city dish with a light broth. Noodles include udon (light-flavoured, springy), soba (cheap buckwheat noodles, very popular) and ramen (dense-flavoured). Sashimi and other seafood plates are prized for freshness. Sakura Mochi and Sakura Tempura use sakura blossom flavour.

Item text describes soba as made from inexpensive ingredients with a simple method, which is why ordinary Inazumans like it. Udon is contrasted with ramen: where ramen prizes dense flavours, udon uses light ones. Tonkotsu Ramen is described as slow-prepared meat over springy noodles in a bone-based soup that is fragrant but not greasy. Rice Cake Soup is said to have started with few ingredients and grown more elaborate over time, and its text calls it a warming dish for a snowy night. Sashimi Platter is presented as an art of knife work and freshness. Sakura Mochi is a delicate sakura-scented sweet with a leaf wrapper. In local folklore, bake-danuki pretend to offer food and shelter while really handing over leaves and mud.

Tricolor Dango is coloured with Sakura Bloom and Snapdragon, and its text links it to watching blossoms and hoping for a good year. Dango Milk, a street-stall creation sold by Tomoki in Inazuma City, is dango added to milk; its text says customers who tried it love it but warns that too much may spoil the appetite. Sakura Blooms are a local specialty gathered from petals around the Grand Narukami Shrine, and travelling cooks consider them excellent for cooking. Crops are hard to grow on Watatsumi Island and in Konda Village.

Regional variation: Documented food culture is concentrated in Inazuma City on Narukami Island (Kiminami Restaurant in Hanamizaka, Shimura's, Tomoki's stall) and relies on seafood from the surrounding waters. Watatsumi Island's poor soil and Konda Village's farming difficulty appear as scarcity rather than as named regional dishes. No source read names a distinct Tsurumi Island cuisine; the island has no living inhabitants after its former civilisation was destroyed.

Characters from elsewhere in the archipelago have their own taste notes: Kazuha, a seafaring wanderer, says fish is the easiest food to get at sea and cares about cooking it well; Kokomi of Watatsumi favours simple Bird Egg Sushi, which she calls well suited to army life; Thoma likes cooking Rice Cake Soup in a big pot to share.

Scene use: Use small, concrete details: a counter at Kiminami Restaurant, dango from a stall, steam from udon, the scent of sakura in a sweet.

Treat food as a warm, ordinary social moment. Inazumans are matter-of-fact about food and can be a little shy about favourites. Let outsiders notice how light the dishes are. Keep flavours and ingredients plausible from the item texts; do not invent elaborate rituals or etiquette that canon does not state.

A scene during the closed-country period can reflect scarcity and tension; a scene after the reopening can include foreign dishes, as when Kiminami Anna adds a pizza to her menu and then tries variations based on customer feedback.

Examples: Ayaka and the Traveler dining at Kiminami Restaurant while Ayaka prepares a pizza as a gift. Yoimiya offering her homemade dango. Thoma ladling Rice Cake Soup for a group. Kirara ordering Sashimi Platters. Kokomi eating Bird Egg Sushi as a soldier's meal.

10.content:
Kiminami Restaurant is a well-known restaurant in the Hanamizaka area of Inazuma City, run by its owner Kiminami Anna. It sells Inazuman classics and recipes such as Soba Noodles and, since Ayaka's story quest Food From Afar, a Mushroom Pizza from abroad; the in-game notice asks customers to thank a friend who helped bring it. Anna says the Kamisato siblings have long sent staff to order her food, and that Ayaka had never before booked a dinner with friends. The owner's home adjoins the restaurant.

In the follow-up quest Pizza From Another Land, Anna asks the Traveler for help because customers are bored of one pizza and want other flavours, and her own attempts have not satisfied them. The pizza version the Traveler did not make in Food From Afar (Mondstadt-style or one using Inazuman ingredients) is then developed and added to her menu after feedback from a customer. It is a clear example of foreign cooking being adopted into Inazuman food culture.

11.content:
Shimura's is a popular eatery in Inazuma City's shopping district, run by Shimura Kanbei. The map description calls him a poor but self-made samurai who finally gained a small fief of his own there. The shop sells simple food, ingredients and recipes such as udon, ramen, miso soup, egg roll and sushi.

The shop description invites passers-by to take food to go if they lack time for tea. Its advertisement board is a running joke that the drinks are good.

12.comment: Inazuma Cuisine: Tricolor Dango and Dango Milk
12.content:
Tricolor Dango is a steamed ball of glutinous rice flour coloured with Sakura Bloom and Snapdragon; its recipe is sold by Kiminami Anna. Gorou lists it as a favourite. Dango Milk, sold by the street vendor Tomoki, who advertises creative cooking, combines dango with milk.

Yoimiya says she prefers snacks to full meals and offers homemade dango to friends. The Dango Milk text says customers who tried it all love it but cautions against drinking too much.

13.comment: Inazuma Cuisine: Sakura Bloom and sakura dishes
13.content:
Sakura Blooms are petals fallen from the Sacred Sakura at the Grand Narukami Shrine, floating in the air under the effect of Electro energy. Cooks use them in sweets such as Sakura Mochi and in savouries such as Sakura Tempura, whose recipe comes from the Gourmet Supremos quest line.

The Gourmet Supremos begin their Inazuma storyline trying to get past a barrier to collect Sakura Blooms, which Xudong has heard have the best mouthfeel for cooking. The culture page calls sakura a flavour unique to Inazuma.

14.comment: Inazuma Cuisine: Noodles and Rice Cake Soup
14.content:
Udon, soba and ramen are staples of Inazuma City's eateries. Soba is cheap and popular, udon is light and soothing, ramen is rich. Rice Cake Soup is a separate savoury rice-cake dish and is Thoma's favourite food.

Udon's text says it uses light flavours to heal the Inazuman soul. Tonkotsu Ramen's text praises the springy noodles and a soup that goes down gently.

15.content:
Xudong (a cook from Liyue), Parvaneh (a scholar from the Sumeru Akademiya) and Julie (an adventurer from Mondstadt) are travelling food-lovers who call themselves the Gourmet Supremos and arrive in Inazuma to improve their cooking with local ingredients. Their quest series gives the Traveler recipes such as Sakura Tempura and Sashimi Platter, and later brings in Kamei Munehisa, a former samurai of the Shogun's Army, as their bodyguard.

Their Inazuma line is unlocked after Ritou Escape Plan. When Parvaneh suggests putting up a commission as Xudong would have in Liyue, Xudong replies that they are strangers in Inazuma; the Traveler happens along instead.

16.content:
Daily Life in Inazuma (also: Inazuman customs, Inazuman way of life, Life in Inazuma): Daily life in Inazuma is an island society of samurai families, shrine and festival calendars, family-run shops and fishing and farming villages, all administered through the Tri-Commission under the Raiden Shogun. Before and as the Traveler arrived (the Vision Hunt Decree had been in force for about a year), the Sakoku and Vision Hunt decrees made it tense, poor and closed; once both ended, the nation reopened to visitors and trade.

Rice, seafood, sakura, books, fireworks and swordsmanship are the recurring textures. Pride and honour matter a great deal, especially among samurai, and the shrine, clan and commission someone answers to shape much of what an ordinary person can do. Watatsumi Island and the Shogunate islands follow different faiths and governments, though both count as Inazuma.

Inazuma has only one major city, Inazuma City, where most of the population lives, and one port, Ritou; the rest of the people live in small villages and estates, some now abandoned after disasters. The decree years left scars: scarce goods, fear of the Tenryou Commission, ships lost in the storm belt, and families with Visions deciding whether to hide them.

Practice: Everyday matters run through three commissions. Tenryou handles security, Kanjou handles borders and documents (checking foreigners and returning citizens), and Yashiro handles shrines, festivals and culture. Samurai houses send children into the Shogun's army and guard their honour, rice and seafood are the staples, and most towns have a shrine nearby.

- **Work and trade.** Printing is a main trade, led by the Yae Publishing House, known across Teyvat for its "This Novel Is Amazing!" contest. Inazuma also exports kimonos, toys and fireworks. An NPC calls Naganohara Fireworks, Yoimiya's family business, one of the oldest and best firework shops in the country. Smithing is another famed craft, with Jade Steel from Tatarasuna in its finest swords, although that production has halted since the peace between Watatsumi and the Shogunate. Jakotsu Mine closed after a "sickness" and Mikage Furnace after its core went critical, so many people hesitate to return to either.
- **Farming and food.** Rice is the staple grain, eaten steamed or pounded into cakes. Seafood is central and noodles are popular. Sakura gives dishes a flavour found nowhere else, as in sakura mochi and sakura tempura. Poor soil limits farming on some islands, including Watatsumi and around Konda Village. Watatsumi's people explain bleaching soil as "Holy Soil" and hold the Watatsumi Mitama Omatsuri against it, while a shrine maiden who studied at the Akademiya thinks salty seawater is the cause.

- **Homes and buildings.** Aralia, maple, otogi and yumemiru wood are the common timbers; yumemiru is used for shrines.
- **Honour.** Samurai families are common and proud. Losing to someone, or needing an outsider's help, is felt as shame.
- **Dress.** Kimono-style garments are everyday wear. Fishers are known by their wide kasa hats, shrine maidens wear a kosode with a hakama that is red on Narukami Island and blue on Watatsumi Island, and soldiers wear ashigaru-style uniforms. Clans carry crests (mon), as the Kamisato and Kujou do.
- **Sayings.** A national motto praises the Shogun's everlasting reign. Inazumans who leave the country for training sometimes call themselves "shugenja".
- **Governance.** The Tri-Commission is led by three great clans: Hiiragi (Kanjou), Kujou (Tenryou) and Kamisato (Yashiro). Inazumans compare it to the Liyue Qixing and the Eight Trades. When a commissioner falls, their clan loses standing and subordinate clans compete for the post, causing instability. The Yashiro commissioner also directs the Shuumatsuban, a ninja organisation for intelligence and counter-operations. Watatsumi Island is governed mainly by the Divine Priestess of the Sangonomiya Clan and has its own Watatsumi Army.
- **Armies and ranks.** The Shogun's Army has recruits, captains and samurai. Non-samurai favour polearms, while samurai use swords and bows because the sword is highly regarded.
- **Spiritual neighbours.** Humans are most numerous, but tengu, oni and kitsune live in Inazuma, mostly in seclusion, as the adepti do in Liyue. Bake-danuki are known for pranking travellers by offering food and shelter that turn out to be leaves and mud.
- **Urban life.** Inazuma City, on the southern cliffs of Narukami Island, is famed for a low crime rate and many family businesses; most of the population lives there and it keeps expanding outward. Hanamizaka, north of the river, is one of its three parts alongside Tenryou and Tenshukaku.
- **Lawlessness outside the city.** Treasure Hoarders and masterless warriors such as Nobushi and Kairagi are common in the wilderness.

Eras: **During the decrees (Version 2.0 Archon Quest).** The Vision Hunt Decree (confiscating Visions) and the Sakoku Decree (closing the borders) were both in force. Few goods came in, and some smugglers refused to bring anything to Inazuma. An NPC describes the atmosphere as tense and dangerous. The Tenryou Commission carried out the Vision Hunt and helped enforce Sakoku, and the Kanjou Commission checked everyone entering or leaving and treated ships as a possible means of escape, so sea trade and fishing both declined. Both decrees were in reality part of a Fatui plot to destabilise Inazuma and sell Delusions. A civil war broke out between the Watatsumi Army and the Shogunate.
**After the decrees.** The Vision Hunt Decree was abolished first and corrupt officials were removed. The Sakoku Decree lingered, though restrictions on foreigners were relaxed, and ended after Ei's duel with the Shogun puppet in Transient Dreams. Visitors, trade and foreign contacts returned, and Inazumans were free to travel again. The ceasefire with Watatsumi turned into a peace.

Regional variation: - **Narukami Island:** Shogunate culture, the Grand Narukami Shrine, sakura, the capital and most family businesses; shrine maidens in red.
- **Ritou:** the outlying island port, and the only legal way in for foreigners during Sakoku. Kanjou Commission officials processed documents here, and visitors could not leave on foot without a Travel Permit, which the Traveler eventually obtained in the quest Chisato's Letter.
- **Watatsumi Island:** worships Orobashi rather than Ei, under the Sangonomiya Clan; blue shrine robes, poor soil, its own army and the Mitama Omatsuri ritual.
- **Yashiori, Kannazuka, Seirai:** Yashiori and Kannazuka are Shogunate islands. Seirai has no permanent residents after the Thunder Manifestation destroyed it, and Higi Village and a village south of it were evacuated after Tatarigami energy was released.
- **Tsurumi Island:** part of the archipelago but empty of people since its Thunderbird civilisation was destroyed by Kapatcir.

Festivals: Festivals shape the calendar, and the Yashiro Commission handles many of them. The Summer Festival on Narukami Island centres on the Naganohara fireworks show, and Yoimiya is sometimes called its queen. The Irodori Festival honours the Five Kasen, poet-singers of ancient Inazuma, and was revived after Sakoku. The Mikawa Flower Festival was once a youkai gathering over five hundred years old. The Goshintou Ceremony offers masterwork swords to the Grand Narukami Shrine, and the Warrior's Spirit Swordfighting Exhibition tests swordsmen, with an emissary standing in for the Shogun.

Duels: Disputes can be taken to the Shogun as a Duel Before the Throne, fought at Tenshukaku and witnessed by her. The duel continues until one side cannot go on, and the loser dies, by a lethal blow or by execution with the Musou no Hitotachi. Kazuha's friend challenged the Shogun over the Vision Hunt and lost this way, and the Traveler challenged Signora in the same form. Treat it as a grave formal procedure, not a casual brawl.

Scene use: Open with sensory detail: sakura petals, grilled fish or sweet dango, shop signs, shrine bells, boats, or thunder over the sea. Locals are polite but proud about clan, craft and honour, and they know the commissions by name. Pick the era first, because before and after Sakoku have very different moods.

- During the decrees: tense and careful, guarded talk, few imported goods, Visions kept hidden, travellers questioned by officials.
- After: warmer and busier, with foreign goods, curious visitors, festivals and light novels in conversation.
- A Watatsumi islander should not use Narukami customs automatically, and the reverse.
- Clerks and guards speak in terms of commission, clan and permit; pride rather than hostility is the usual tone.

Concrete settings include a Hanamizaka street, the Yae Publishing House shop, the Ritou customs office or a fireworks stall. Do not invent laws, prices or holidays beyond what is listed here, and keep scenes at or before Version 7.1.

Examples: - A shopkeeper in Inazuma City mentions a new light novel from the Yae Publishing House and points to the fireworks hanging in a stall, saying the Summer Festival will soon be here.
- A Kanjou Commission clerk in Ritou, during Sakoku, asks a visitor for their papers and says they cannot continue on foot without a Travel Permit.
- A Watatsumi islander hopes the Mitama Omatsuri will slow the bleaching of their fields.

17.content: The Tri-Commission administers Inazuma for the Shogun. The Tenryou Commission, led by the Kujou Clan, handles internal and external security; its commissioner Kujou Takayuki was dismissed over the Fatui plot, Kujou Kamaji acts as proxy and Kujou Sara commands the Shogunate forces. The Kanjou Commission, led by the Hiiragi Clan, handles borders and documents; Hiiragi Shinsuke was dismissed after supplying the Fatui, and Hiiragi Chisato appears in the Travel Permit quest (Chisato's Letter). The Yashiro Commission, led by the Kamisato Clan under Kamisato Ayato, handles shrines, festivals and culture and directs the Shuumatsuban.

18.comment: Daily Life in Inazuma: Ritou and the Travel Permit
18.content: Ritou is the Kanjou Commission's processing centre for non-Inazumans. During the Sakoku years foreigners could not leave Ritou on foot without a Travel Permit, though Fatui and Snezhnayan merchants were at first exempt because of diplomatic ties. The Traveler eventually received a permit from Kujou Kamaji in the quest Chisato's Letter.

19.comment: Daily Life in Inazuma: Yae Publishing House
19.content: A leading publisher in Inazuma and across Teyvat, founded by Yae Miko, with a contest called "This Novel Is Amazing!" Its notice board advertises Zhenyu's Liyue work A Legend of Sword and a search for editors who like light literature, and Albedo's artwork is said to interest the house. Yae Miko is editor-in-chief, known as Lady Yae.

20.content:
Duels in Inazuma (also: Duel Before the Throne, duel before the throne, Inazuman duels, Gozenjiai): A duel before the throne is Inazuma's formal way to settle a grievance. The challenger brings the dispute to Tenshukaku, the Raiden Shogun's residence in Inazuma City, and fights the other party there with the Shogun as witness. By the account of the wiki's culture page, the duel ends when one combatant cannot fight on, and the loser dies: struck down, or executed by the Shogun's Musou no Hitotachi. Samurai also settle matters of pride with informal sword duels.

Canon shows the formal duel twice. Kazuha's friend, an Electro Vision bearer, challenged the enforcers of the Vision Hunt Decree and lost to Kujou Sara, who accepted on the Shogun's behalf. In the Archon Quest Duel Before the Throne, the Traveler invoked the same law against the Fatui Harbinger Signora and won. Anyone who calls the duel takes on a fight to the death.

Practice: Someone who believes they have been wronged challenges the offender, and both go to Tenshukaku and state their case to the Raiden Shogun. If she permits it, they fight until one cannot continue. The loser does not walk away.

The Shogun's permission matters: in the Archon Quest scene she simply says "Proceed" and the fight begins. The victor may leave Tenshukaku alive, and the Shogun states that she acknowledges the winner's honour. Before the duel, Signora reminds the Traveler that the loser must die and asks whether they are sure; the Traveler does not retreat.

The loser is either killed outright in the fight or, if they survive, executed by the Shogun with the Musou no Hitotachi, the sword technique the people of Inazuma regard as unanswerable. In the Archon Quest the defeated Signora threatens consequences from Snezhnaya; the Shogun disregards this and carries out the sentence anyway, calling Signora an enemy of eternity while recognising the victor's honour. The setting adds weight: Tenshukaku was built during the Archon War and also houses the Tenryou Commission's headquarters, so the duel takes place at the seat of power itself.

Regional variation: The formal duel is specific to Inazuma and to the court at Tenshukaku. The more ordinary form is the samurai's duel of pride. Samurai families have a strong sense of honour, and being beaten in a fight or needing an outsider's help is typically treated as shameful. The world quest Dreams of Sword Art shows a nameless samurai who demands to fight the Traveler repeatedly while searching for something he has forgotten.

No equivalent formal duel before a ruler is described for Mondstadt, Liyue, Sumeru or Natlan in the sources read here. Fontaine has its own legal duelists, covered in a separate entry on the Champion Duelist, and they should not be merged with the Inazuman custom.

Scene use: Use it as a high-stakes, solemn law: a character invoking it is deadly serious, onlookers go quiet, and the challenged party must answer. Do not treat it as a casual spar.

A challenge needs a grievance and a venue. Inazuman characters who know of the custom see it as binding and fearsome, and Kaedehara Kazuha has particular reason to grieve it. Keep the Shogun's permission and the lethal outcome in view, and let characters weigh them.

For ordinary samurai quarrels, a sword duel can be a matter of face rather than law, and the stakes can be anything from a lost argument to wounded pride. Mark the difference between the two: one is judged by the Shogun, the other is not.

Examples: Kazuha's friend lost a duel before the throne against Kujou Sara and was executed. The Traveler defeated Signora in a duel before the throne.

Kazuha's friend had asked Kazuha about the Musou no Hitotachi, learned it was the Shogun's pinnacle technique, and made it his ambition to overcome it. His challenge to the Vision Hunt enforcers led to the duel, which Kujou Sara accepted on the Shogun's behalf. Kazuha arrived after it was over and took his friend's dying Vision.

In the Archon Quest the Traveler follows Sara to Tenshukaku, where Signora has already knocked her unconscious. The Traveler's challenge is accepted, a hard fight follows, and Signora, after emerging in a second form, is beaten. The Shogun then executes her with the Musou no Hitotachi and says the Traveler may leave alive. Soon after, in the same quest line, the Shogun strikes at the Traveler anyway, and Kazuha blocks the blow using his own Anemo Vision and his dead friend's Electro Vision.

21.comment: Duels in Inazuma: Duel Before the Throne
21.content:
Inazuma's formal duel, fought in Tenshukaku before the Raiden Shogun. A challenger presents a grievance, the Shogun grants permission, and the fight continues until one side cannot go on. The loser dies, killed in the duel or executed by the Musou no Hitotachi. The victor may leave alive.

In the Archon Quest of the same name, the Traveler challenges Signora in this way and defeats her. The Shogun executes Signora and honours the winner's right to leave.

22.comment: Duels in Inazuma: Kazuha's friend and the duel
22.content: A former Electro Vision bearer and close companion of Kaedehara Kazuha. He wanted to overcome the Musou no Hitotachi and challenged the Vision Hunt Decree's enforcers to a duel before the throne. He lost to Kujou Sara, who accepted for the Shogun, and was executed. Kazuha took his dying Vision.

23.content:
Inazuma Fashion (also: Inazuman fashion, Inazuman clothing, Inazuman attire, Inazuma clothing): Dress in Inazuma is recognisably kimono-based and varies by age, work and allegiance more than by region. Ordinary townsfolk wear everyday attire in a handful of patterns for men, women, children and the elderly; kimono proper marks the better-dressed. Fishers have no special costume but are picked out by their kasa. Soldiers of the Shogun's Army and the Watatsumi Army wear foot-soldier uniforms in their own colours with their masters' crests, and shrine maidens wear a standard kosode-and-hakama outfit, red on Narukami Island and blue on Watatsumi Island. Fabric trade runs through shops such as Ogura Textiles & Kimonos in Inazuma City, whose supply of imported silk and local dye was disrupted by the Sakoku Decree.

Fashion also shows up as a living trade. The Ogura shop is a century-old family business serving samurai families, and its owner is trying to find new patterns and dyes to keep customers. Inazuman tailoring is also where the Fontaine designer Chiori started out, which gives the craft a link to the wider world.

Practice: **Ordinary dress.** NPC models show separate patterns for children, men, women and the elderly, with plainer everyday clothes and fuller kimono for the well dressed. Wiki observers note that women often have bangs, younger women a short bob and older women their hair tied up in a bun; this is a pattern in the models, not stated in game text.

**Fishers.** Fishers do not have a distinct costume; the wide kasa hat is what marks them.

**Samurai and fighters.** Samurai-style clothing and armour appear on enemy groups such as the Kairagi and the Nobushi, who are told apart mainly by colour palette and by the kind of kasa they wear (the Jintouban wear a conical Nirayama-style hat).

**Shogun's Army.** Rank-and-file soldiers are modelled on feudal ashigaru: a shirt (shitagi), loose trousers (kobakama), white socks and straw sandals (waraji), plus eggplant-coloured armour bearing the Shogunate crest, and a cross-shaped spear (juumonji yari) with a lavender shaft. Officers have fuller sleeve armour and sometimes a jingasa hat with the crest. Higher samurai such as yoriki carry a katana on the left hip and wear a helmet and shoulder armour. Community study reads rank from colour: low ranks in purple-grey and grey, officers with lavender trousers and pale-gold trim, yoriki and above in lavender and indigo with dark-gold trim.

**Watatsumi Army.** A single uniform design serves the whole army: a shirt in a red-to-white gradient with a red-violet left sleeve, grey trousers, sandals without socks, and red-and-black armour with gold accents. The Sangonomiya crest is printed on the back of the shirt and on the right shoulder guard and under the spearhead of the red-and-white spear.

**Shrine maidens.** The standard outfit is a kosode and hakama with white socks and okobo sandals. Maidens of the Grand Narukami Shrine on Narukami Island wear red hakama and red accents; maidens of the Sangonomiya Shrine on Watatsumi Island wear blue.

**Cloth, silk and dye.** The shop Ogura Textiles & Kimonos says that before the Sakoku Decree it could buy high-grade Liyue silk, including silk woven from Silk Flowers by the Feiyun Commerce Guild. With foreign trade shut, its owner says merchants lost their businesses, the dye houses of Ritou closed, and dyes grown in Konda Village no longer sold for good prices. Liyue silk became scarce and expensive, and the shop worked through old stock. After the story of Transient Dreams, she says contacts with suppliers have yet to be re-established, so stock is still limited.

**Clothing as social signal.** The shop notes that upper-class samurai are regular customers, and the owner presents an Inazuma-style outfit as a natural thing to offer a well-travelled outlander. Foreign silk is described in-world as a glimpse of how people live elsewhere.

Regional variation: The clearest regional split is institutional rather than geographic: shrine maidens and soldiers dress in the colours of the power they serve. On Narukami Island, shrine maidens wear red hakama and the Shogun's Army wears eggplant armour with the Shogunate crest. On Watatsumi Island, maidens wear blue and soldiers a red-white gradient with the Sangonomiya crest. Everyday dress in the rest of the islands follows the same kimono-based vocabulary, with fishers distinguished by kasa.

Konda Village and Ritou matter to fashion through dye rather than costume: Konda grew dyes and Ritou had dye houses, both damaged by the closed-country years according to the Ogura shop's owner.

Scene use: - A tailor's shop is a natural place for small talk about the Sakoku years, scarce silk and what the customers are asking for.
- Describe soldiers by uniform colours and crest rather than by name; the crest tells the player whose authority stands behind them.
- A foreign visitor in outlander clothes stands out, and shopkeepers may offer Inazuma-style outfits as a friendly gesture.
- Keep garment names to the ones above; avoid inventing named clan patterns or ranks that canon does not give.

For a fashion-minded scene, the commission with Ogura Mio gives an in-world hook: she wants new dyes and novel kimono patterns. Other outlanders she asks suggest books and tea sets as designs, and she is receptive to unusual dye materials.

Examples: - Maki of the Grand Narukami Shrine and Izumi Naki of the Sangonomiya Shrine: shrine maidens in red and blue outfits.
- Watanabe, Kobayashi and Okawara Goemon: Shogun's Army soldier, officer and yoriki attire.
- Teppei: standard Watatsumi Army attire.

24.content: A family-run shop in Inazuma City, said to have existed for about a century, selling fabrics and the latest kimonos; upper-class samurai are regular customers. Ogura Mio runs it alone because her brother Yuu was called into the Shogun's Army and is in Kannazuka. The shop's notice says imported Silk Flowers are out of stock because of the Sakoku Decree and invites advance orders, with work to begin when silk returns. In the daily commission Crash Course on Inazuman Fashion, Mio asks the Traveler for ideas for new dyes or patterns. According to the Ogura Mio wiki page, which cites Chiori's Vision story, Mio studied tailoring alongside Chiori and invited her to work at the shop; Chiori declined but was moved by the offer.

25.content: Standard Shogun's Army dress is modelled on feudal foot soldiers: shirt, trousers, white socks and straw sandals, with eggplant-coloured armour bearing the Shogunate crest and a cross-shaped spear with a lavender shaft. Officers may wear a crest-marked jingasa; yoriki add a helmet and shoulder armour and carry a katana. Rank colours are a community reading of the models.

26.content: One uniform design for the whole Watatsumi Army: red-to-white gradient shirt with a red-violet left sleeve, grey trousers, sandals without socks, and red-and-black armour with gold accents. The Sangonomiya crest is on the back of the shirt and the right shoulder guard.

27.content: Shrine maidens wear a kosode and hakama, white socks and okobo sandals. Those of the Grand Narukami Shrine wear red hakama; those of the Sangonomiya Shrine on Watatsumi Island wear blue.

28.content:
Religion in Inazuma (also: Inazuman religion, Inazuma faith, worship of the Shogun, Narukami faith): Faith is visible in daily Inazuma life. The Shogunate islands worship the Raiden Shogun (the Electro Archon) through the Grand Narukami Shrine and the Sacred Sakura; Watatsumi worships the serpent god Orobashi; Tsurumi's Thunderbird cult died out long ago.

Shrine maidens, torii gates, fortune slips and seasonal rites are everyday sights. The faith is tied to politics: the Shogunate's decrees, the Vision Hunt and the Sakoku, made worship of the Shogun and loyalty to the state hard to separate, while Watatsumi's separate devotion fed the island's quarrel with the Shogun. Since the decrees were lifted in the Archon Quest, shrines have kept their ordinary duties; the practices below describe the state of things as of 7.1.

Three different relationships with the divine coexist in the archipelago. The Shogunate islands venerate a living Archon whose protection is symbolised by a tree. Watatsumi honours a god that Ei killed, and treats it as a guardian because it taught its ancestors farming and smelting after finding them in the Dark Sea. Tsurumi's tribe fed a being that never asked for worship. Canon leaves the second and third cases unflattering to the gods concerned.

Practice: The Grand Narukami Shrine, Inazuma's largest, crowns Mt. Yougou beneath the Sacred Sakura and is dedicated to the Raiden Shogun. Yae Miko leads it. Visitors pray and draw fortune slips.

The shrine is outside the Shogunate's jurisdiction and answers to the Electro Archon; military force near it is not permitted because it would dishonour the Shogun. Its duties include receiving worshippers, guarding the Sacred Sakura and the Thunder Sakura, and holding rituals and ceremonies, above all the Sacred Sakura Cleansing Ritual. The sakura is read as the Archon's watch over Inazuma. Its branches, the Thunder Sakura, absorb filth into the roots, and because the roots cannot purge themselves the filth must be cleansed at intervals. A five-petalled sakura flower is the shrine's emblem and appears on Yae Miko's clothing. Most shrine maidens in Inazuma (not Watatsumi) are trained at the Grand Narukami Shrine, and tending local shrines keeps them aligned with it; the Kuki Clan has long supplied shrine maidens there. While the Sakoku was in force, a shrine maiden recounted that many visitors came to pray for it to end because it had hurt their livelihoods. The shrine maiden's outfit is a kosode with hakama, white socks and okobo sandals, with red hakama on Narukami Island.

Fortune slips: a visitor shakes a bamboo slip from the box and exchanges it with the shrine maiden Gendou Ringo for a fortune slip; one per day, and the previous day's slip loses meaning. Ill-omened slips (Misfortune, Great Misfortune) may be tied to a hanger as a prayer for a turnaround; the item text adds that fate is best forged in one's own hands.

Goshintou Ceremony: a solemn event honouring the arrival of the Shogun, said to have brought swordsmithing to Inazuma, at which master smiths offer their finest blades (goshintou) to the Grand Narukami Shrine (book Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi).

Warrior's Spirit Swordfighting Exhibition: in the past champions faced the Shogun herself with an "Emissary of the Archon"; today she sends an emissary instead (most recently Kamisato Ayaka). It is a martial rather than priestly event, linked to the Archon's honour.

Hyakkiyakou: the "night parade of a hundred demons", once a gathering of youkai organised by the Kitsune Saiguu that grew from a storytelling party; it had not been held for centuries until Yae Miko held a farewell version in The Great Narukami Offering (see its entry below).

Regional variation: Shogunate islands: Shogun and Sacred Sakura. Watatsumi Island: Orobashi, the Watatsumi Omikami. Tsurumi Island: the ancient Thunderbird cult, now extinct.

Watatsumi: the island was created by Orobashi after the Archon War, its giant corals are said to be branches broken from Orobashi's body, and the people of Enkanomiya who climbed them to the surface are the ancestors of the Watatsumi people. They worship Orobashi instead of the Raiden Shogun, under the Sangonomiya Clan. Orobashi attacked the archipelago, which tradition ties to the island's scarcity of resources, though the deeper cause given is that the Heavenly Principles had condemned it for learning forbidden knowledge; Ei killed it on Yashiori Island about 2,000 years ago, and the Sangonomiya Clan sought peace. Ei allowed Watatsumi to keep honouring it. Shrine maidens there are trained at the Sangonomiya Shrine and wear blue rather than red. Sangonomiya Kokomi is the Divine Priestess and also leads the Watatsumi Army.

Orobashi's legacy: on Yashiori Island its slaying left the Musoujin Gorge and its remains, and its lingering will and power became the Tatarigami, a curse that causes storms, illness and madness when the wards over it fail. This is why worship of Orobashi is not purely benign in canon: the same god is a guardian to Watatsumi and a calamity on Yashiori.

Watatsumi Goryou Matsuri (Mitama Omatsuri): a ritual that holds off the "Holy Soil" bleaching and erosion of Watatsumi's land (which legend attributes to the depths of Enkanomiya drawing on the island's spirit), requiring a Jade Coral Branch from Enkanomiya, itself made from Orobashi's body. After the Three Realms Gateway Offering, Kokomi decided to look for a way to avoid disturbing the vishaps and ease the need for it.

Under the Vision Hunt Decree hostility rose between the Sangonomiya Clan and the Shogun's followers, particularly the Tenryou Commission; after it was abolished, talks on returning the island to Shogunate rule began and then stalled when the Fatui's influence on the Shogun's Army came to light.

Scene use: Shrines give atmosphere: torii, red-clad maidens, fortune slips. Watatsumi feels different: blue-clad maidens, coral, reverence for Orobashi.

Watatsumi's feeling toward the Shogunate's old rule has softened but not vanished. Characters from the Shogunate islands usually speak of the Shogun with respect and distance; Watatsumi characters do not credit the Shogun with their protection. Do not turn Orobashi worship into villainy: locals revere it, while the Tatarigami suffering on Yashiori is a separate consequence. Fortune slips are a light, repeatable scene beat; the Cleansing Ritual is a heavier one involving the Grand Narukami Shrine and Hanachirusato.

Avoid giving the Raiden Shogun a modern-day sermon or a miraculous response to prayer; the shrine's daily business is run by Yae Miko. Ei's own view of her godhood and of Eternity is covered in her character entries, so keep this entry to the practice of worship.

29.comment: Religion in Inazuma: Grand Narukami Shrine Worship
29.content:
The Grand Narukami Shrine at the summit of Mt. Yougou is Inazuma's largest shrine, dedicated to the Raiden Shogun as the Almighty Narukami Ogosho. Yae Miko oversees it; worshippers pray, draw fortune slips and seek the Archon's blessing. It is independent of the Shogunate's jurisdiction and answers only to the Electro Archon. Shrine maidens from across the Shogunate islands are trained there. See the faction entry for its people.

Its history reaches before the Archon War; its first attendant was the kitsune Hakushin, and about 500 years ago it was led by the Kitsune Saiguu and the Great Tengu.

30.content:
A huge sakura on Mt. Yougou that purifies Inazuma's ley lines and keeps Abyssal corruption out. Sakura Bloom petals across Narukami Island fall from it, and its protection is said to extend wherever they rest. Its roots interconnect all of Inazuma's sakura into one organism; the Thunder Sakura (side branches) absorb filth that must be cleansed in the Sacred Sakura Cleansing Ritual. Locals once believed it cleansed the land of impurity.

According to Ei, the tree began from a seed Makoto gave her in a realm of consciousness, and took root in the past; Ei came home from Khaenri'ah to find it already standing on Mt. Yougou and everyone saying it had always been there. Yae Miko's altered memory kept Ei from convincing her. The tree has probably fused its roots with the Irminsul's (a domain description), which would explain its glow. Its fox-like form is attributed by Yae Miko to centuries of care by kitsune. Origin is disputed in the uncertainties.

31.comment: Religion in Inazuma: Sacred Sakura Cleansing Ritual
31.content: Ordinarily the Grand Narukami Shrine's job. In the world quest series the Traveler and the masked shrine maiden Hanachirusato lift five barriers and purge the filth in each, then destroy a tumor under the sakura. Hanachirusato is revealed to be filth condensed from the Kitsune Saiguu's memory, and she disperses with the cleansing. Without cleansing, the interconnected roots corrode and form tumors.

32.comment: Religion in Inazuma: Watatsumi Omikami and Sangonomiya Faith
32.content:
Watatsumi worships Orobashi, the serpent god it calls the Watatsumi Omikami, as its guardian because it taught the first islanders to farm and smelt. Sangonomiya Kokomi serves as Divine Priestess. Shrine maidens train at the Sangonomiya Shrine and wear blue. The shrine now standing was built after Orobashi's death. Orobashi died around 2,000 years ago, slain by Ei.

The Goryou Matsuri holds off the erosion of Watatsumi's soil using a Jade Coral Branch made from Orobashi's body.

33.content: The curse born from Orobashi's will and power after its death on Yashiori Island. With the wards broken it brings perpetual storms, withered crops, mysterious illness and hallucinations. Vision-bearers and those with elemental sensitivity are somewhat protected. Its victims often speak of a terrifying god called "Him".

34.comment: Religion in Inazuma: Thunderbird Cult of Tsurumi
34.content:
Tsurumi Island's tribe worshipped Kanna Kapatcir with blood sacrifices. After the youth Ruu was sacrificed, she destroyed the tribe in rage and cursed the island to repeat the event. Ei later killed her. The curse was broken in the Traveler's Tsurumi quests (The Sun-Wheel and Mt. Kanna) when Ruu sang to her remains.

The tribe used Ishine Script and a Maushiro made of her feathers. The wiki names Kama as the sole living descendant; check the quest text before using him.

35.comment: Religion in Inazuma: Hyakkiyakou and the Kitsune Saiguu
35.content: This is event material (The Great Narukami Offering). Yae Miko holds a last Hyakkiyakou, a spirit-sending ritual for youkai memories, for her old friend Urakusai and others, after Transient Dreams damaged the ley lines. The Kitsune Saiguu originally organised the gatherings; she died about 500 years ago during the Cataclysm.

36.content:
Inazuman Script (also: Inazuma script, Inazuman alphabet, Inazuman writing, Ishine Script, Tanuki language): The Inazuman script is the writing seen on Inazuma's shop signs, posters, book covers and charms. The game never names it. It is a stylised alphabet that mostly writes romanised Japanese, usually reduced to the first letter of each syllable, so a sign for a festival ("omatsuri") may read only OMTR. It can run top to bottom, right to left, or sideways. Tsurumi Island has a separate, canon-named Ishine Script that only priestly families knew.

Inazuman letters correspond to Latin letters, and some Inazuman texts are even in English. The script is the Inazuman counterpart of the scripts of other nations, and it sits alongside the common Teyvat script rather than replacing it.

Practice: Signs name a shop by its trade or name in abbreviated form. Examples read by fans: KM for the Komore Teahouse, ST for a bathhouse (sentou), KJ for the Amenoma Smithy, NTK for Netsuke no Gen Crafts. Book covers use the same compressed shorthand, as with SGNMYA on the Sangonomiya Chronicles.

Reading is a matter of guessing from context. Per fan analysis, only the first letter of each syllable is usually written, so ka, ki, ku, ke and ko all share one symbol; voicing is often ignored; long vowels and the final n are often dropped; and there are no spaces or capital letters. A few letters (L, Q, V, X) turn up with inconsistent values. Many texts therefore do not match the official Japanese transcription of the same text. In a scene, an Inazuman sign is a quick label, not a place to hide a full paragraph of exact words.

- Directions: vertical top to bottom and right to left, as on Mysterious Flyers or Idol Posters and in Arataki Itto's burst animation (AK ONI, taken to mean "red oni"), or horizontal, as on the Yellowed Letter.
- Longer prose is rendered as strings of consonant-heavy letters, as on the Official Tenryou Commission Document. These are hard even for fans to decode, which fits the compressed, shorthand feel of the script.
- Calligraphy: Kamisato Ayaka's calligraphy in her character teaser is written vertically in the script.
- Some items use plain alphabetic Latin in the same style: a queue sign near the Kousaka stall reads "Queue here", and during the Irodori Festival event (2.6, limited-time) the title was written in the script as a transcription of its Japanese name.

Regional variation: The script is Inazuma's; nothing in canon says it is used outside it. In other nations, other scripts (the common Teyvat script, the Liyue, Sumeru, Fontaine and Snezhnayan styles) appear.

Tsurumi Island is the exception inside Inazuma: its old civilisation had the Ishine Script, written glyphs known only to priestly families, used for names of people and places. It is a different writing system from the Inazuman script and is not the same thing under another name.

Canon in the 2.2 Octave of the Maushiro quest shows that the glyphs survived on carved stones and cliffs: stones must be struck in the order of the script on a cliff wall, and the stone-tiles must be matched with the same glyphs. In a hidden exploration objective called Ishine Script Deciphering (unofficial name; 2.2), seven Stone Slates are collected from Mysterious Carvings around Tsurumi Island and placed in carvings in the ruins under Chirai Shrine; a "Seven Letters" achievement is attached.

Tanuki speech: The tanuki (bake-danuki) of Inazuma also have a spoken language of their own, though no script is attested. According to Ioroi, tanuki can understand human speech by nature but speak their own tongue among themselves. In the 2.0 world quest Tanuki-Bayashi in the Forest, a magical food prepared by Ioroi lets the Traveler follow some of it, though much still sounds like nonsense (the tanuki Kichiboushi is rendered as "squelch squelch lavender melon"). Ioroi explains the nonsense as the Traveler not yet being used to Kichiboushi's aura, and the wiki notes that talking to him grows clearer over the quest.

This is the only description of the tanuki tongue, and it comes from one quest. Treat it as flavour, not a system: do not invent tanuki words, only describe it as garbled and aura-dependent.

Scene use: Use the script as background colour: a shop sign in a few angular letters, a poster or a book spine whose title is only a handful of symbols. A character who can read it simply does; an outsider from other nations may only guess at it.

- A Traveler or outlander reading Inazuman signs should have to guess, or ask, rather than read fluently; a local reads the shorthand without effort.
- Avoid inventing a full grammar, a long translated text, or "ancient secrets" in the ordinary Inazuman script. Keep any decoded sign short and plausible: a trade word or name.
- Ishine glyphs belong to Tsurumi Island and to its past; canon shows the knowledge was restricted to priestly families.

- A mysterious cipher scene is better served by the Ishine glyph puzzles (stones struck in order, tiles matched) than by inventing rules for Inazuman shorthand.
- Keep the tanuki speech vague: gibberish that gradually clears as the listener adapts.

Examples: Read as fans do: OMTR is "omatsuri" (festival), KJ is "kaji" (smithing), OMR is "omamori" (charm), SK for "shoukai" (trade association) on the International Trade Association sign. Each is a guess from context, not an official translation.

- SGY for the Bantan Sango Detective Agency is read as "Sango, ya" (shop).
- KOUKA SUGATQ NO IDORVRX SAI is read as the Irodori Festival title during the 2.6 limited-time event, showing that Q and X can stand in for other letters.
- The line IROHANIHOETO CHIRINURUO from the event is read as the opening of the Iroha poem, an ancient Japanese poem used as a pangram (limited-time event content).

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the script appears unchanged and unexplained in the sources read: canon has never named it, taught its rules or translated it. The Ishine Script remains a Tsurumi-only matter from 2.2, and no source read ties either script to any content in 6.x or 7.0-7.1.

37.content:
The Inazuman script is the community's name for the writing on signs, posters, books and charms throughout Inazuma. It looks like a stylised alphabet, mostly spelling out romanised Japanese by its first letters (KM for Komore, OMTR for "omatsuri"), written vertically or horizontally. Readings are educated guesses; canon never explains the script.

Besides signs, it appears on a floor mechanism in the Relics of Seirai, the Official Tenryou Commission Document, the Yellowed Letter, a festival promotion poster and Arataki Itto's burst animation. In the 2.6 Irodori Festival event it carried the event title.

38.content: The Ishine Script is the written language of the old civilisation of Tsurumi Island. In the 2.2 quest Octave of the Maushiro, illusions of its people say that its knowledge was passed only through priestly families, and that it was used to name people, places and things on the island. Puzzles in the quest and a hidden objective require matching or ordering its glyphs: striking stones in the order of the script on a cliff wall, matching tiles, and placing seven Stone Slates into carvings in the ruins under Chirai Shrine. The meaning of the glyphs is never translated in-game.

39.content: Per Ioroi in the Chinju Forest, tanuki understand human speech naturally but have their own tongue. His magical food lets the Traveler follow part of it; the rest comes out as gibberish ("squelch squelch lavender melon" from Kichiboushi), which Ioroi blames on the Traveler not yet being used to that tanuki's aura. Speech with Kichiboushi becomes clearer as the quest goes on.

40.content:
Irodori Festival (also: Magnificent Irodori Festival, Kouka Sugata no Irodori Sai, The Five Kasen Plaza): The Irodori Festival is an Inazuman arts festival that honours the Five Kasen, five legendary poets of ancient Inazuma who were gifted in song and verse and whose collections were once presented to the Shogun. It faded from memory over the centuries. After the Sakoku Decree was lifted, Yae Miko and the Yashiro Commission revived it in Ritou as an "international cultural festival" built around light novels, with guests invited from other nations.

Its one confirmed modern edition is the "Magnificent Irodori Festival" of Version 2.6. Nothing in canon says it is a regular yearly fixture.

Practice: The festival exists to show appreciation for the Five Kasen, whose works are said to have sparked cultured discussion and made Inazuma's culture blossom. In legend, one of the five presented a new poetry collection to the Shogun at Tenshukaku each year, and stories about the group were long popular, often as stage plays in which each Kasen wore one colour: green, blue, red, white and black. The revived festival swaps poetry for the modern equivalent, light novels, showcased with official and fan-made works, giveaways, prizes and new-release parties.

In the 2.6 edition the main exhibition space surrounded the Outlander Affairs Agency in Ritou, with stalls selling light-novel merchandise. The small plaza in front of the International Trade Association became "The Five Kasen Plaza", where five blank boards waited for portraits of the Kasen painted by an artist invited from Mondstadt. The Yashiro Commission lodged invited guests at the International Trade Association and wanted guides who knew both Inazuma and the other nations. Other event activities centred on writing poetry, floral arrangement, staged mechanical theatre and martial contests, all offered as festival pastimes.

History: The Five Kasen brought a cultural flowering to ancient Inazuma, and the Irodori Festival grew out of the people's gratitude for their works. As their tales were gradually forgotten, so was the festival. Yae Miko revived it once the Sakoku Decree was abolished, in the Hues of the Violet Garden event (2.6, April 2022); Ayato calls it the first major Inazuman festival since the decree was lifted. She admitted that her fondness for light novels shaped the choice of format, while also arguing that a living culture needs a modern medium.

Information about the Five Kasen is scarce, and the Five Kasen Summary blames the great calamity five hundred years ago for much of the loss. The festival's name echoes the real kabuki piece Rokkasen Sugata no Irodori, according to the wiki; this is an out-of-universe etymology.

Story 2 6: During the Hues of the Violet Garden event the Traveler and Paimon were commissioned by Yae Miko to act as guides for foreign guests arriving at Ritou's docks. The guests included Venti, Albedo (painting the Kasen portraits), Xingqiu (author of the novel "A Legend of Sword") and Kaedehara Kazuha. According to the wiki, Albedo's portraits were modelled mainly on the invited party, with the blank-looking Kuronushi portrait based on Scaramouche (now the Wanderer). Copies of Xingqiu's latest volume went missing, and a series of poems telling a new version of the Kasen legend appeared around town.

Kamisato Ayato revealed that he wrote the poems himself and used the legend to guide Kazuha toward a secret left by Kaedehara Yoshinori; the clues, including ink that appears only with water and the hidden Kuronushi portrait, led Kazuha to the truth about his family. Miko had originally asked Ayato only to tease the editor and Xingqiu after seeing them smuggle books out at night. This is an event-only story, so characters outside it would not necessarily know of it.

Scene use: Use the Irodori Festival as a cultured, slightly eccentric setting: poets and novelists on holiday, serious scholars mixing with enthusiastic fans, Yae Miko pursuing her publishing interests under cover of tradition. It is a good scene for introducing a foreigner to Inazuman arts, or for a character who is nervous about being in public. Keep it tied to Ritou and the post-Sakoku opening of Inazuma.

Reasonable hooks include a missing manuscript, a rival guest arriving by ship, or an odd poem that seems to point toward a buried family secret. Do not treat the festival as a fixed annual event, and do not assign the original Kasen real names or works.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the revived festival has been held once in canon (2.6). The Five Kasen remain legendary, with no confirmed identities.

41.content:
The Five Kasen were gifted poets and singers of ancient Inazuma whose works stimulated its culture. Their names are colour-based stage names from plays: Suikou (green), Aoi no Okina (blue), Akahito (red), Sumizome (white) and Kuronushi (black). Their true names and exact lives are lost, and accounts vary, so treat any detail as legend. The wiki notes the group parallels the real-world Rokkasen, six famous Japanese poets of the ninth century.

In the Hues of the Violet Garden event the version told to the party is Ayato's invention, and Albedo painted portraits based on the party. Kuronushi's portrait had to be splashed with water to reveal its secret.

42.content:
Mikawa Flower Festival (also: Mikawa Festival, Akitsu Haneasobi, Akitsu Yuugei): The Mikawa Flower Festival was a lively festival held by Inazuma's youkai, an occasion to drink, laugh and play music, in the days when the Hyakkiyakou still wandered the night. Its highlight was Akitsu Haneasobi, a game played with hagoita (decorated wooden paddles). The tradition dates back more than five hundred years, and Ei, her sister Makoto, Kitsune Saiguu and Yae Miko are among those said to have attended. It has since been revived twice in modern Inazuma: first as a small festival by three young youkai (Version 3.3), then as a larger festival for humans and youkai alike organised by Yae Publishing House (Version 5.4).

The festival is remembered above all as a place where youkai and humans could simply have fun together. Its legend of a samurai and a youkai who became lifelong friends over a game is the heart of how it is retold today.

Practice: In the old festival, youkai gathered to eat, drink, make music and play games. Akitsu Haneasobi, played with hagoita to hit a ball toward a target, was its centrepiece, and the game had long been lost by the present day. Ei remembers it as once quite popular at festivals, and Makoto enjoyed playing it. The modern versions replace it with invented games: Akitsu Yuugei (3.3), a flipper-and-brick game on the beach, and, in 5.4, games made by attendees themselves, including "Akitsu Harpastum".

The festival's meaning in tales retold today is friendship between humans and youkai and gratitude between them. Youko, the youkai who retells the legend, calls Akitsu Haneasobi "a symbol of friendship" and says the festival is meant to bring happiness to all who attend. Food stalls are central to the modern editions, and in 5.4 the proposed proceeds split gave forty percent to Yae Publishing House and ten percent to the festival representative (Raiden Shogun's account).

History: More than five hundred years ago youkai held the Mikawa Flower Festival, and prominent youkai, Ei, Makoto, Kitsune Saiguu and Yae Miko were among the guests. One year a human samurai, Yanagibashi Takuto, stumbled into the festival. The youkai debated how to make him leave, but a youkai named Kamai Kenji declared that the point of the festival was to have fun, offered him sake and played Akitsu Haneasobi with him, ending in a draw. They agreed to meet for a duel every ten years, and their friendship shaped the sword style Takuto later founded, the Souran Isshin Art.

According to Hanyuuda Chizuru, Takuto was about twenty-five when they met; they met again ten years later, and when Kamai next saw him Takuto was sixty-five and too weak to finish a last game of Akitsu Haneasobi. Five hundred years ago, Kamai fought beside Tominaga Masanari, third-generation heir of the Souran Isshin Art, until their final moments, wielding a sword handed down from Yanagibashi, resolving the regret Kamai had once felt. Miko followed Kitsune Saiguu around the festival one year and saw the hagoita pair then.

Modern revivals: In 3.3 Kamisato Ayato set up the Test of Courage on Narukami Island after learning that three young youkai, Youko, Kappa and Hitotsume Kozou, wanted to hold their own Mikawa Flower Festival. They lacked the youkai power for a full festival, so they spent most of what they had on Akitsu Yuugei, their reconstruction based on the legend, and set up a few stalls in the forest. Strange hauntings during the event traced back to Hanyuuda Chizuru, the spirit of an old hagoita pair, whose slumber the three youkai's game had woken and who had used her fading youkai power to scare off a man trying to steal decorations from Akitsu Yuugei. At the end Arataki Itto took over organising a proper festival, which was held with the Traveler's friends in attendance.

Ei, who visited the Test of Courage, recalled the old festival and Makoto's fondness for it. The three youkai said they wanted to thank the humans who had driven off monsters and allowed youkai to live in peace.

Festival 2025: In 5.4 Yae Miko, with the Raiden Shogun's approval, appointed the Traveler as festival representative for a larger Mikawa Flower Festival open to all humans and youkai, run by Yae Publishing House and aiming to combine human ingenuity with youkai arts. The core of the festival was a two-day game-making contest. Rumours of doppelgangers at the venue, stories of a threat from a dream-linked creature called a Nightmare Fragment, and a plan by Miko, the Kamisato siblings, Ei and Yumemizuki Mizuki to use dream against nightmare, made up the story event; the festival then went ahead, and an organiser reported three times the usual number of visitors.

The bake-danuki, including Kichiboushi, Shousei and Gyoubu Koban, took part in the festival after Miko's personal invitation, despite the grumbling of Ioroi in Chinju Forest. The games made for it included the Akitsu Harpastum (Thoma's blend of Akitsu Yuugei and Mondstadt's Ludi Harpastum), and a "Tanuki Game Award" went to the winning booth. Shikanoin Heizou says the Tenryou Commission sent soldiers to stay undercover on the festival grounds. The event is limited-time content, so it is optional knowledge for characters.

Scene use: Use it as a nostalgic setting for older characters (Ei, Miko) or for a warm, slightly mischievous youkai scene. Games, stalls and sake are always on offer; a human newcomer may be met with suspicion that melts when the host stresses that the festival is for fun. It is also a natural place to bring up the old days of the Hyakkiyakou.

The tone is best kept light and friendly, with a vein of wistfulness: friends who die and friendships that outlive them. Do not claim a fixed date or location, as each canon edition used a different site (the beach on Narukami Island in 3.3, a venue by Chinju Forest and Mt. Yougou in 5.4).

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the festival has been revived twice (3.3 and 5.4). No later edition or regular calendar is established.

43.comment: Mikawa Flower Festival: Kamai Kenji and Yanagibashi Takuto
43.content: A youkai (Kamai Kenji) and a human samurai (Yanagibashi Takuto) became friends after playing Akitsu Haneasobi at the Mikawa Flower Festival and agreed to duel every ten years. Their duels fed into the Souran Isshin Art, which Takuto founded. Kamai later befriended Tominaga Masanari, third-generation heir of the style, and died fighting at his side five hundred years ago.

44.content: Hanyuuda Chizuru is the spirit of the hagoita pair Kamai and Takuto played with, born of long exposure to great youkai power. She felt proud to have left a mark on their story, but her rotting body left her hiding from humans and using scare tactics. Yae Miko first saw her at the festival and sensed her youkai power on the beach before the 3.3 event.

45.content:
Summer Festival (also: Inazuman Summer Festival, Naganohara Fireworks Show, Queen of the Summer Festival): In Inazuma, fireworks mean summer. The summer festival on Narukami Island is a night of masks, stalls, fortune slips, darts and water balloons, ending with the Naganohara Fireworks Show over Inazuma City, which Naganohara Fireworks supplies. Its owner Yoimiya is called the "Queen of the Summer Festival", and people say summer on Narukami Island would not be the same without her.

The show is a communal event: families light their own favourite fireworks from paper slips the Naganoharas prepare, and Yoimiya chooses the moment for the grand finale.

Practice: Festival-goers wear masks, an old custom that is now only optional, and browse stalls for fortune slips, prayer plaques, throwing darts and water balloons. The fireworks show is the one constant across Inazuma's recurring festivals. The Naganohara family prepares fireworks for each participating family, with paper slips holding the recipes for what they ordered; people light their chosen fireworks, and the owner of Naganohara Fireworks stages the grandest display at the right moment. In summer people sit on Amakane Island to watch the display over Inazuma City.

Fireworks mean different things to different people: friendship for some, marriage for others, belief for others still. Yoimiya says she has never settled what they mean to her but that people's feelings give them purpose. Yoimiya herself falls silent while watching the show, calling it a sacred ceremony. Yashiro Commission staff, with shrine maidens, handle fire precautions so that she can work freely, and Takami of the Commission helps manage the show on Amakane Island.

History: Over a century ago the Yashiro Commission organised a commemorative fireworks display made by the best pyrotechnicians of the time, which is regarded as the origin of the Naganohara Fireworks Show.
